name: Compound Umami — The Synth-Cuisine Breakthrough of 2203
creator: Dr. Yewande Achampong-Brandt, HelixCorp Food Sciences Division
description: In 2203, HelixCorp food scientist Dr. Yewande Achampong-Brandt published a process for synthesizing what she called Compound Umami — a fifth-generation synth-protein base that, for the first time, replicated not just caloric and nutritional content but the full Maillard reaction flavor profile of slow-braised animal protein, including the specific volatile compounds responsible for the 'long finish' quality that had previously only existed in real meat. The process was immediately licensed across all major synth-food producers and within 18 months had become the baseline standard for Tier 2-3 synth-protein products. At Φ0.06 per gram more expensive than previous synth-protein, it was not accessible at true Tier 1 poverty levels, creating a flavor gap that became its own social flashpoint.
cultural_impact: Compound Umami is credited with a measurable improvement in food satisfaction scores across Tier 2 populations and a significant reduction in the cultural shame attached to eating synth-protein, because the product was now genuinely good rather than merely adequate. It also accelerated the collapse of the lower end of the real-meat market, as the price premium for genuine animal protein became harder to justify on flavor grounds alone.
controversy: Dr. Achampong-Brandt received a HelixCorp Innovation Bonus of Φ40,000 for the discovery; the process itself was patented by HelixCorp and generates an estimated Φ800 million annually. She has publicly stated that she considers the compensation arrangement unjust and has donated most of her bonus to the Gray Zone food cooperatives, but cannot legally challenge the patent.
story_hooks: An independent food scientist claims to have found an undisclosed compound in the Compound Umami base that has mild neurological effects — not harmful, but technically constituting unauthorized BCI-adjacent stimulation — and HelixCorp's legal response has been swift and disproportionate.

Dr. Achampong-Brandt is quietly working on a second-generation process that she intends to release open-source, outside HelixCorp's patent framework, and she needs help getting it to market before the company finds out.

A Tier 1 community food cooperative has reverse-engineered an approximate version of Compound Umami using geneware-modified yeast strains — technically patent infringement — and has been feeding 2,000 people per week on it for eight months.
